query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Parts made from a refractory high-entropy alloy, such as the equiatomic Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20, will exhibit enhanced resistance to corrosion and erosion when exposed to high‐temperature liquid aluminum compared to conventional materials used for hot-dip aluminum plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, processed high-entropy alloy (e.g., as-cast followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing to induce a beneficial microstructure with a dispersed HCP phase)
generation.intervention: Fabricate or coat dipping/plating equipment parts with the Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 high-entropy alloy
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature (∼700–750°C) liquid aluminum during hot dip plating operations
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure that develops during processing (e.g., formation of a dispersed HCP phase via HIP), which contributes to increased hardness and high-temperature strength
generation.mechanism: The refractory elements in the alloy promote the formation of protective oxide layers and provide high-temperature stability, thereby reducing the rate of erosion and chemical attack by molten aluminum
generation.predicted_outcome: Parts made from or coated with the high-entropy alloy should show lower mass loss and surface degradation over time in molten aluminum than conventional materials, potentially extending service life significantly
generation.baseline: Conventional materials (such as standard steels or low-grade alloys) currently used in dipping/plating equipment, which suffer accelerated corrosion under molten aluminum exposure
generation.boundary: The benefit is predicted under conditions typical of hot dip aluminum plating; however, the brittleness at room temperature and potential issues related to ductility or thermal shock resistance remain unquantified
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the inherent brittleness observed in tensile testing and the abnormal crack propagation noted in prior studies will negatively impact performance in a real-world molten aluminum environment. The degree and longevity of protective oxide formation in the high-entropy alloy under these conditions also remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of test samples fabricated from the Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 high-entropy alloy using the same processing route (e.g., casting followed by HIP) and a matched set of conventional material samples. Expose both sets to industrially relevant molten aluminum environments for extended cycles. Monitor surface degradation, mass loss, and microstructural changes over several cycles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., reduced mass loss, surface degradation, and longer service life) compared to conventional materials, then the hypothesis that their use offers enhanced protection is falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads.
